subtopic: An unrealistic deadline from a manager
subtype: Approach: offering scope options instead of a flat no [Action]
passage:
Note for my file, engineering manager. On Monday I asked Nitya for the whole payments feature in two weeks. Nitya did not say no. On Tuesday Nitya came with a one-page sheet holding three options: A, the whole feature over six weeks; B, the main payment path in two weeks, with settlement checked by hand each day; C, a two-week prototype that real customers would not use. Each option had a line on what it cost and what it risked. I asked which Nitya recommended. B, with reasons. I chose B and told the sales team. Then I took two other tasks off Nitya's plate and booked the daily manual check with the finance team.

Vikas

qa.q: Which option did the manager choose?
qa.a: The manager chose option B, the main payment path in two weeks with settlement checked by hand each day.

qa.q: How might Vikas have felt on seeing three options instead of a plain no?
qa.a: Vikas was probably relieved and impressed, since the options turned a refusal into a decision Vikas could make.

qa.q: What else could Nitya do to help the manager decide, and why?
qa.a: Nitya could state a clear recommendation with reasons, as Nitya did, because a recommendation saves the manager from guessing which option is safest.

qa.q: How might Nitya have felt when the manager chose option B?
qa.a: Nitya probably felt heard and relieved, since the choice fit what Nitya recommended and came with two tasks removed.

grounding: Illustrates bringing a manager three scope options, a full build, a core flow with manual checking and a prototype, instead of a flat no.

subtopic: An unrealistic deadline from a manager
subtype: Approach: offering scope options instead of a flat no [Action]
passage:
Tuesday night.
Today I did the thing I've been dreading: the payments deadline talk.
My manager wanted the whole feature in two weeks. My breakdown says six. Simran told me last week, "Don't just say no. Give him choices." So I did.
I walked in with a single page and three options.
One: the full feature, all banks, refunds and reports, in six weeks.
Two: the core flow only, customers can pay by card, in two weeks, and finance reconciles by hand at the end of each day until the rest is built.
Three: a clickable prototype in two weeks for the investor meeting, no real payments.
He read it twice. Asked who would do the manual reconciliation. I said finance had agreed to one person for a month. He picked option two.
I'm still tired, but for the first time this month I don't feel like I'm lying to anyone.
Gurleen

qa.q: Which option did the manager pick?
qa.a: He picked option two, the core flow in two weeks with manual reconciliation.

qa.q: How does Gurleen feel after the meeting?
qa.a: Gurleen feels tired but relieved, not feeling like lying to anyone for the first time that month.

qa.q: What else could Gurleen do to make option two work?
qa.a: Gurleen could agree a clear plan with finance for the manual work and a date for the full feature, so the temporary fix doesn't drag on.

qa.q: How might the manager see Gurleen's three options?
qa.a: The manager gets real choices instead of a flat no, which makes it easier to decide and trust Gurleen's estimates.

grounding: Shows a developer bringing the manager three scope options instead of refusing: the full feature later, a core flow with manual reconciliation, or a prototype.
